tldr: Researchers developed a rotating knuckle mechanism where fingers independently travel around a cylindrical palm via a belt drive. They proposed ORBIT, a modular robotic hand platform that reconfigures finger layouts and numbers without hardware rebuilding to enable fair comparisons across hand morphologies.
hero_caption: Overview of ORBIT mounted on a Franka robot arm. By rotating the finger roots on the same hardware, it can switch in under 1 s to diverse hand morphologies, such as (A) Anthropomorphic (two fingers opposing an offset thumb), (B) Isometric (three fingers spaced at 120°), and (C) Barrett-style (two fingers opposing a centered thumb).
overview:
In robotic hand research, diverse morphologies have been proposed, ranging from human-like to non-anthropomorphic multi-fingered designs. However, for fundamental questions like "how many fingers are optimal?" or "where should the thumb be placed?", there has been no common platform to perform direct "apples-to-apples" comparisons across different morphologies under identical actuators, control, and test conditions.

To address this, the authors developed ORBIT (Orbital Reconfigurable Base-actuated Integrated Theta-motion Hand), a modular robotic hand that dynamically alters finger layouts. Its core innovation is a rotating knuckle mechanism: individual finger carriages independently orbit along a circular V-rail on a cylindrical palm via a timing belt. Finger modules can also be attached or swapped easily, allowing changes in finger count, geometry, and placement angles without rebuilding the entire hand.

In hardware characterization, the finger bases demonstrated rapid movement with an average angular velocity of 1.57 rad/s, as well as a robust root finger force resistance of 50 N. Using a three-finger configuration of this mechanism, the authors reproduced anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style layouts to perform grasping experiments and grip force measurements across 11 household objects.

The results clearly mapped tasks to their optimal morphologies: anthropomorphic suited objects with offset centers of gravity, isometric suited symmetric shapes like spheres, and Barrett-style suited axially symmetric tools. Furthermore, by using this orbital degree of freedom directly during manipulation, the hand demonstrated complex tasks, including precision pinching of sub-millimeter screws, sub-second cube face reorientation without learning, and unscrewing jar lids without wrist rotation.
contributions: Development of a rotating knuckle mechanism where fingers independently travel around a cylindrical palm via a belt drive, reconfiguring finger layouts dynamically in under 1 s
Implementation and characterization of a modular 3-finger robotic hand combining 2-DOF bio-inspired linkage fingers with a compliant artificial palm

A fair morphological comparison experiment measuring grasp force and grasping performance across 11 objects by reproducing three representative finger layouts (anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style) on the same hardware
Demonstration of dynamic manipulation using the orbital base DOF, achieving precision pinching of sub-centimeter screws, high-speed cube face reorientation, and lid unthreading

sections.heading: Why hasn't there been an "apples-to-apples" comparison of hand morphologies?
sections.summary: Multi-fingered hands range from anthropomorphic to non-anthropomorphic designs, but disparate hardware has prevented fair performance comparisons. This section outlines the concept of ORBIT—a modular hand that reconfigures layouts by rotating finger bases—and the paper's core contributions.
sections.details:
To achieve dexterous robotic manipulation, many multi-fingered hands using tendon drives or linkage drives have been developed. Prominent examples include the BarrettHand, Allegro Hand, and LEAP Hand, yet their thumb placements and dimensions vary widely. Recently, non-anthropomorphic hands with symmetrically spaced fingers around the palm and designs with unconventional degrees of freedom (DOFs) have emerged. Still, clear answers remain elusive for questions like "which morphology is ultimately optimal?" or "is the added complexity of non-anthropomorphic mechanisms truly worthwhile?"

This issue persists because prior hardware was tailored for single design targets. There has been no platform capable of comparing different morphologies directly using the same motors, identical links, and identical control conditions.

To solve this, the authors introduce ORBIT (Orbital Reconfigurable Base-actuated Integrated Theta-motion Hand). Finger carriages independently orbit the perimeter of a cylindrical palm, enabling dynamic adjustments to finger layout angles, geometry, and finger counts without disassembling or redesigning the hand. This provides a direct, controlled benchmark to evaluate the pros and cons of different hand morphologies.

sections.heading: Fingers orbiting a cylindrical rail: ORBIT's mechanism and modular design
sections.summary: This section details the rotating knuckle mechanism at the core of ORBIT, along with the end-effector units consisting of 3D-printed linkage fingers and a compliant palm. Adapting 3D-printer V-rail principles to a cylinder achieves multi-directional load capacity and rapid modular swapping.
sections.details:
### II-A Rotating Knuckle Mechanism
The core of ORBIT is the rotating knuckle mechanism, which applies linear V-rail principles from 3D printers to a cylindrical form. Because commercial cylindrical V-rails do not exist, the two-part base cylinder was 3D printed from PLA (Polylactic Acid). Splitting it into two bolted sections allowed support-free, high-precision printing of the V-grooves, ensuring smooth carriage travel and reduced wheel wear.

While typical linear V-rails bear loads primarily in one direction, robotic hands face multi-directional moments during grasping. To withstand these, each carriage mounts opposing V-wheels in a triangular arrangement, creating a rigid structure that evenly distributes external forces and moments. Each carriage houses a compact DC gearmotor with a 25:1 reduction ratio to drive along a single shared timing belt (MXL standard). The carriages serve as mutual belt tensioners, allowing independent actuation of all fingers on a single belt.

Swapping a finger module requires only unplugging a connector and removing two screws. Adding or removing fingers simply requires adjusting the belt length, providing high modularity for morphological exploration.

### II-B Hand Instantiation
For the experimental platform, a 3-finger hand was configured to balance simplicity and versatility. Each finger possesses 3 degrees of freedom (DOFs):
- **DOF 1 (Base Orbital Motion)**: Driven by the DC motor to orbit around the cylindrical palm.
- **DOF 2 (Adduction/Abduction)**: Driven by a servomotor at the base for side-to-side yaw (analogous to human MCP lateral motion).
- **DOF 3 (Flexion/Extension)**: Driven by a servomotor via a cascaded four-bar linkage mechanism for curling/extension (analogous to human PIP/DIP joints).

Each fingertip is equipped with a 5 mm compliant sponge pad, friction tape, and a 1 mm protruding rigid PLA "nail" at the tip. This nail slips under thin objects or miniature parts where rounded pads would slip. In addition, joint backlash and sponge deformation introduce passive compliance, allowing fingertips to adapt naturally to object geometries without complex force control.

At the center of the palm, a compliant palm mimics human cushions like the thenar and hypothenar eminences. 3D-printed with Formlabs Silicone 40A, it improves power grasps. Distributed Arduino Nano units and motor drivers on each carriage handle control, receiving target angles from a host PC over serial communication.

captions.F3: Demonstration of ORBIT's modularity. Swapping a standard finger for a shorter thumb module requires removing just two screws. Adding or removing fingers is easily accommodated by sizing the timing belt.

sections.heading: Measuring baseline performance: sub-second travel and 50 N load resistance
sections.summary: Experiments evaluated the positioning accuracy, operating speeds, and load resistance of the rotating knuckle mechanism and linkage fingers. Morphology switches across maximum angles completed in under 0.6 s, and fingers held position against 50 N without belt slippage.
sections.details:
### III-A Rotating Knuckle Mechanism Characterization
Performance was evaluated with carriages fixed on the robot arm in gravity-neutral orientations.
- **Positioning Accuracy**: Motor encoder data was compared against external video tracking. With the PID dead-band set to ±30° at the motor shaft (about ±2.0° carriage angle), the system reached steady state in 0.6 s, reliably settling into the dead-band without overshoot.
- **Angular Velocity**: Transition times among the three test morphologies were measured via video. Carriages reached an average angular velocity of 1.57 rad/s and a peak of 2.36 rad/s. Even the largest morphology transition (76.6°) took under 0.6 s, showing that any layout reconfiguration completes in less than 1 s.
- **Load Resistance**: External forces perpendicular to the orbital direction were applied to the finger base. In 9 out of 10 trials, the carriage held firm up to the 50 N limit of the force gauge without shifting (slipping occurred at 42 N in only one trial). This demonstrates sufficient structural stiffness for grasping.

### III-B Finger Unit Characterization
Individual fingers were clamped in a vise to test behavior across their full range of motion (20° to 160°).
- **Positioning Accuracy**: DOF 2, being direct-drive, exhibited minimal deviation below measurement limits (max error < 2°) and high stiffness. DOF 3, actuated via linkages, had a maximum fingertip position error of 5.04 mm at the travel limits due to accumulated joint backlash, closely matching the kinematic model.
- **Operating Speed**: Traversing the full 140° range took 0.53 ± 0.01 s for DOF 2 and 0.96 ± 0.09 s for linkage-driven DOF 3. The slight delay in DOF 3 stemmed from linkage friction and deceleration profiles near joint limits.

These results confirm that base orbital travel (DOF 1) is fast and strong enough to serve not just for static reconfiguration, but as an active primitive during dynamic manipulation.

sections.heading: Comparing 3 morphologies: specialized strengths and the power of orbital motion
sections.summary: Anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style layouts were evaluated on the same hardware through grasp force tests and grasping trials across 11 objects. Actuating the finger bases during tasks (orbital DOF) further enabled precision pinching of micro-screws and rapid cube face reorientation.
sections.details:
### IV-A Grasp Force Comparison
Grasp forces were measured across the three layouts (Anthropomorphic: 20°/60°/270°, Isometric: 0°/120°/240°, Barrett-style: 345°/75°/210°) by commanding maximum finger flexion onto load cells fitted with a spherical jig (25 mm diameter) and a flat jig (20×40 mm).

The anthropomorphic layout recorded the highest grasp force. Because its two adjacent fingers oppose the thumb at a nearly perpendicular angle, normal force transmission is maximized. By contrast, the isometric and Barrett-style layouts engage contact surfaces at oblique angles, yielding lower normal force components.

### IV-B Grasping Evaluation on 11 Objects
Experiments tested grasping across 11 objects: a chip canister, hat, cracker box, M3 screw, volleyball, five small stacked cubes, earphones, a güiro, a frying pan, a glass, and an electric drill. The routine consisted of arm descent, finger closure to preset angles, lifting 100 mm, and holding for 3 s.
- **Anthropomorphic**: Displayed superior stability on asymmetric objects with offset centers of mass like the frying pan and drill. The offset thumb resisted gravitational tipping moments effectively.
- **Isometric**: Excelled at grasping large spheres like the volleyball and groupings of five small cubes, as the three 120°-spaced contact points applied balanced forces toward the geometric center.
- **Barrett-style**: Performed best on tools requiring longitudinal balance, such as the güiro. Its centered opposing thumb allowed level lifts without tilting. Its broad DOF 2 yaw range also provided flexibility to emulate traits of the other two layouts.

All three static layouts failed on the 430 g cracker box (insufficient fingertip friction) and on the flat-lying M3×5 mm screw (fingers could not converge tightly enough with fixed bases).

### IV-C Dynamic Manipulation via Orbital DOF
To overcome static limits, DOF 1 was actuated dynamically during task execution.
- **Precision Pinching of Micro-Screws (M3×5 mm)**: Moving two carriages together over the screw allowed the rigid PLA nails to slip beneath the screw head before curling the fingers, picking it up cleanly.
- **In-Hand Cube Face Reorientation**: Starting from an isometric grasp on a 5 cm cube, rotating all three carriages +30° simultaneously reoriented the cube face by 90° in under 1 s—without requiring complex reinforcement learning policies.
- **Jar Lid Unthreading**: In an isometric grasp on a peanut butter jar lid, continuous counter-clockwise rotation of all carriages unscrewed the lid entirely using hand DOFs alone, without arm or wrist rotation.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook: morphological optimization and the path to sim-to-real
sections.summary: ORBIT demonstrates that multi-fingered hand morphologies can be compared fairly on a single platform. Future directions include integrating tactile sensing and force control, optimizing morphology in simulation, and validating sim-to-real transfer on physical ORBIT hardware.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated ORBIT, a modular robotic hand platform capable of dynamically changing finger layouts via an independent rotating knuckle mechanism. By reproducing three prominent hand morphologies (anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style) under identical mechanical and actuation constraints, the work clarified their specialized grasp strengths and mechanical properties. Furthermore, utilizing base orbital motion (DOF 1) during manipulation proved to be a versatile primitive for in-hand reorientation and precision pinching.

Looking ahead, the authors highlight several research avenues:
- **Advanced Sensing and Active Control**: Integrating fingertip tactile sensors and moving beyond position control to force-controlled grasping algorithms.
- **Simulation-Based Morphology Optimization**: Algorithmically optimizing foundational design variables—such as finger count, finger DOF layouts, and palm profiles—for target tasks in simulation.
- **Sim-to-Real Hardware Validation**: Leveraging ORBIT's modularity to reconfigure hardware to match simulation-optimized forms and empirically validate them in real-world settings.

Beyond serving as an individual end-effector, ORBIT functions as a valuable testbed for exploring the fundamentals of robotic hand morphology and embodiment.

takeaways: ORBIT provides a shared benchmark platform to answer "which hand shape is best?" by altering finger layouts while holding actuators and control systems constant.
Task geometry dictates the best morphology: anthropomorphic suits tools with offset centers of gravity, isometric suits spherical objects, and Barrett-style suits axially balanced tools.
Orbital finger-base motion serves not only as static layout reconfiguration but also as an active manipulation primitive for unscrewing lids, spinning cubes, and pinching micro-objects.
Adapting linear 3D-printer V-rails into a cylindrical form with triangular wheel supports is an effective approach to building a lightweight yet rigid rotating base capable of resisting 50 N.
limitations: Current control relies on independent PID position control without force feedback or tactile sensing, leading to grasp slips on heavier items (e.g., a cracker box) due to insufficient normal force.
Changing the finger count requires manually swapping timing belt lengths, meaning finger count adjustments are not yet fully automated.
Spur gears and linkages in the finger flexion mechanism introduce mechanical play, accumulating up to 5 mm of backlash error at travel extremes.
